title: "Do authors update their papers after Unjournal evaluations?"
author: "The Unjournal"
date: "2026-04-17"

A key question for any evaluation process is whether it actually changes anything. Do researchers engage with the feedback they receive — and do they revise their work as a result?

We have begun tracking this systematically across our portfolio. The results so far are available here:

**[Did Authors Respond to Unjournal Evaluations? (interactive table and analysis)](https://valentinklotzbuecher.github.io/llm-uj-research-eval/paper_response_analysis.html#combined-evidence)**

## What we found so far

Based on manual coding of 57 tracked evaluations (the results snapshot below was last updated in April 2026):

- **19 papers** received a formal or informal author response to the evaluation
- **16 papers** received a formal written response
- **5 papers** show clear evidence of substantive updating after the evaluation, with evidence linking the two
- **7 authors** stated their intention to update
- **15 papers** show at least some positive signal — evidence of updating, a stated intention, or minor revisions

The remaining 35 papers are either too recent for follow-up or pending assessment. These categories describe the evidence we found; they do not establish that an evaluation caused a later revision.

## Improving the comparison checks

The earlier automated comparison was useful for finding candidate cases, but it was not enough to support causal claims. A newer PDF or a large text difference can reflect an unrelated revision, a different document, or a timing mismatch.

As of July 2026, we have refreshed the public sources and are using a more conservative workflow:

- 30 current public paper versions have been captured;
- nine have a preserved before-and-after comparison record; and
- five currently pass preliminary document, identity, and timing checks and are awaiting focused review.

These are workflow-coverage figures, not findings about the effect of evaluations. For each candidate, we now preserve PDF snapshots and hashes, check that the before and after documents are versions of the same paper and are in the right order, and create page- and section-level change cards. Any claim that evaluator feedback contributed to a change still requires human review.

## Ongoing work

This is an evolving project. We plan to extend coverage, refine the document checks, and link observed revisions to specific evaluator suggestions only where the evidence is sufficiently clear. Automated and model-assisted checks are used to organize the review, rather than to make the final call. The table will be updated as new data are reviewed.

The methodology combines manual assessment of author responses and paper revisions with automated PDF comparison. The detailed evidence table and the historical exploratory LLM screen are available in the [interactive analysis](https://valentinklotzbuecher.github.io/llm-uj-research-eval/paper_response_analysis.html#combined-evidence).
